title: HAProxy: Draining a Server Without Dropping a Request
intro: HAProxy is the other proxy you'll meet most, often in front of databases and as a dedicated load balancer. Its advantage for operations is the runtime API: you can inspect and change live state through a socket without touching the config file. The host lb-1 balances the backend named app across the servers app1, app2, and app3. You need to take app2 out for maintenance.

steps.prompt: Check the configuration file /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg is valid.
expected_commands: sudo haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
haproxy -c -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
sudo haproxy -f /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg -c
steps.explanation: The file parses and is consistent.
steps.why: The same discipline as 'nginx -t': check before any reload. Warnings are printed here too, and are worth reading; a common one is a backend with no health check, which means HAProxy will keep sending traffic to a dead server.

steps.prompt: Ask the running HAProxy for the state of its servers, through the admin socket at /run/haproxy/admin.sock.
expected_commands: echo "show servers state" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo "show servers state" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'show servers state' | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'show servers state' | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
steps.fake_output:
# be_name srv_name srv_addr    srv_op_state srv_admin_state srv_check_status
app       app1     10.0.1.11   2            0               L7OK
app       app2     10.0.1.12   2            0               L7OK
app       app3     10.0.1.13   2            0               L7OK
steps.hint: echo "show servers state" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
steps.explanation: All three servers are up (operational state 2), in normal admin state (0), passing layer-7 health checks.
steps.why: Unlike open-source nginx, HAProxy checks its servers actively: 'option httpchk GET /health' requests a URL on a schedule and removes a server that fails before any user request reaches it. L7OK means the HTTP check passed; L4OK would mean only that the port accepts connections, which a hung application still does.

steps.prompt: Put server app2 in backend app into drain mode.
expected_commands: echo "set server app/app2 state drain" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo "set server app/app2 state drain" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'set server app/app2 state drain' | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'set server app/app2 state drain' | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
steps.explanation: app2 gets no new connections; the ones it has continue until they finish.
steps.why: Drain is the polite way to remove a server. 'maint' is the abrupt one: it also stops health checks and is for a server that's already broken. Draining first means no request is cut off mid-flight. Sessions pinned to app2 by a cookie still go there while it drains, which is why long-lived sticky sessions make maintenance slow.

steps.prompt: Wait for it to empty. Show the current sessions for each server: from 'show stat', print the proxy name, server name, and current sessions (fields 1, 2, and 5 of the comma-separated output).
expected_commands: echo "show stat" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,5
echo "show stat" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,5
echo 'show stat' | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,5
echo "show stat" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock | cut -d , -f 1,2,5
steps.fake_output:
# pxname,svname,scur
web,FRONTEND,412
app,app1,208
app,app2,0
app,app3,204
app,BACKEND,412
steps.hint: echo "show stat" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock | cut -d, -f1,2,5
steps.explanation: app2 has 0 current sessions; app1 and app3 are carrying its share.
steps.why: 'show stat' is CSV with dozens of columns, so cut picks the useful ones; scur is current sessions. Check the other two numbers before starting maintenance: the remaining servers now carry 50% more each. If they were already near their limit, taking one out causes the outage you were trying to avoid.

steps.prompt: Maintenance on app2 is done. Put it back into rotation.
expected_commands: echo "set server app/app2 state ready" | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo "set server app/app2 state ready" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'set server app/app2 state ready' | sudo socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo 'set server app/app2 state ready' | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
steps.explanation: app2 receives new connections again, once its health check passes.
steps.why: Runtime changes live in memory only: a reload or restart returns every server to what the config file says. That's usually what you want for maintenance. If a server should stay out, change the file as well. With 'slowstart 30s' on the server line, HAProxy ramps traffic up gradually so a cold application isn't hit with full load at once.

steps.prompt: A config change (a new backend) has been validated. Apply it without dropping connections.
expected_commands: sudo systemctl reload haproxy
systemctl reload haproxy
steps.explanation: A new HAProxy process took over the listening sockets; the old one finishes its connections and exits.
steps.why: Like nginx, reload is seamless and restart is not. The old process stays until its last connection closes, so a long-lived connection can keep an old process, with the old configuration, alive for hours; 'hard-stop-after' sets a deadline. This is one more reason to use the runtime API for routine changes: it needs no reload at all.
